title: NIV Requires an Airway the Patient Can Protect
bottomLine: Noninvasive ventilation depends on a patient who can cooperate, maintain airway protection, and tolerate the interface. Worsening consciousness, inability to clear secretions, repeated vomiting, or rapidly deteriorating respiratory status requires immediate escalation for a more definitive airway/support strategy.
recognize: Declining mental status, ineffective cough, copious secretions, vomiting, severe agitation, or inability to keep the mask in place are danger cues.
priorities: Assess airway protection, breathing effort, oxygenation/ventilation trends, and responsiveness; summon respiratory/medical support promptly when suitability is deteriorating.
assessMonitor: Trend mental status, respiratory rate/work, gas-exchange data as ordered, secretions, mask tolerance, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Position to support ventilation, maintain suction/emergency equipment access, and follow the ordered escalation pathway.
medicationSafety: Avoid using sedating medication simply to force NIV tolerance unless specifically ordered with appropriate monitoring; sedation can worsen airway protection and hypoventilation.
teaching: Explain that the mask supports breathing but requires alert participation.
delegationScope: NIV initiation/settings and escalation are respiratory/medical competency dependent; PN/LVN role emphasizes focused monitoring, comfort support, and urgent reporting.
examTrap: Continuing NIV indefinitely in a progressively obtunded patient because oxygen saturation looks acceptable.
oneLinePearl: NIV only works safely while the patient can protect the airway and the clinical trajectory is improving.
sourceBasis: Official ERS/ATS Noninvasive Ventilation for Acute Respiratory Failure guideline

title: NIV Mask Seal: Fix Leaks Without Injuring the Face
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A major mask leak can reduce effective support, but over-tightening can cause pressure injury and intolerance. Balance seal quality with skin protection and patient comfort while reassessing whether support is clinically effective.
recognize: Persistent leak alarms, dry eyes, facial redness, nasal-bridge pain, blanching, skin breakdown, and poor delivered support are common interface problems.
priorities: Inspect fit and skin, reposition interface per device guidance, and involve respiratory therapy for persistent leak or pressure injury.
assessMonitor: Trend leak, skin integrity, delivered support, comfort, work of breathing, and response after adjustments.
interventions: Use prescribed protective interface/barrier strategies that do not compromise the seal.
medicationSafety: Analgesia may support comfort when indicated but should not mask worsening respiratory distress or pressure injury.
teaching: Ask the patient to report pain, burning, eye irritation, or a sense that the mask is suddenly leaking.
delegationScope: Routine skin checks may be shared; mask/system adjustments beyond trained competency require respiratory/qualified support.
examTrap: Tightening straps repeatedly until the leak disappears despite blanching skin.
oneLinePearl: A perfect seal is not safe if it causes tissue injury.

title: NIV and Vomiting: Aspiration Risk Changes the Plan
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Vomiting while a tight NIV mask is in place can create immediate aspiration risk. Nausea, abdominal distention, emesis, or impaired airway protection require rapid mask removal when safe, suction/readiness, and escalation for alternative support.
recognize: Nausea, retching, gastric distention, reduced alertness, and inability to remove the mask independently increase risk.
priorities: Protect the airway, remove or release the interface promptly if vomiting occurs and the situation permits, suction as needed, and call for help.
assessMonitor: Monitor mental status, emesis, breath sounds, oxygenation, cough effectiveness, and signs of aspiration.
interventions: Follow the prescribed nutrition/NPO and gastric-decompression plan where applicable.
medicationSafety: Administer antiemetics only as ordered; medication does not eliminate aspiration risk in a patient who cannot protect the airway.
teaching: Tell the patient to signal immediately for nausea or vomiting rather than trying to tolerate it silently.
delegationScope: Airway emergency response is immediate; NIV continuation decisions require respiratory/medical reassessment.
examTrap: Leaving the mask tightly secured during active vomiting.
oneLinePearl: Vomiting plus NIV is an airway emergency cue, not a comfort problem.

title: NIV Failure: Worsening Work of Breathing Means Escalate Early
bottomLine: NIV is a trial of support, not a reason to delay definitive rescue. Rising work of breathing, worsening gas exchange, hemodynamic instability, exhaustion, or declining mental status despite support requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Increasing accessory-muscle use, paradoxical breathing, inability to speak, worsening gas-exchange results, falling alertness, or shock indicate failure.
priorities: Recognize trajectory rather than one isolated oxygen reading and call respiratory/medical emergency support early.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate/effort, oxygenation, ventilation markers, mental status, hemodynamics, comfort, and response after each intervention.
interventions: Ensure emergency airway equipment and personnel are available while continuing ordered support as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not mask respiratory fatigue with sedatives/opioids unless clinically indicated and closely monitored.
teaching: Explain that escalation may be needed if the mask is not improving breathing.
delegationScope: PN/LVN should promptly report deterioration; decisions about escalation/intubation and NIV settings belong to qualified clinicians.
examTrap: Waiting for saturation to fall before reporting obvious respiratory exhaustion.
oneLinePearl: NIV success is measured by improving trajectory, not merely by wearing the mask.
sourceBasis: Official ERS/ATS Noninvasive Ventilation for Acute Respiratory Failure guideline

title: COPD on NIV: Watch Ventilation and Fatigue, Not Oxygen Alone
bottomLine: In acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbation, NIV can reduce work of breathing and improve ventilation when appropriate, but oxygen saturation alone does not show whether carbon dioxide retention and respiratory fatigue are improving.
recognize: Drowsiness, headache, worsening confusion, reduced respiratory effort after marked fatigue, persistent accessory-muscle use, or worsening gas-exchange findings can signal ventilatory failure.
priorities: Monitor mental status, work of breathing, ordered blood-gas/ventilation data, and overall response; escalate deterioration promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory effort, oxygenation target per order, ventilation markers, secretions, mask tolerance, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Support prescribed bronchodilator, secretion-clearance, positioning, and NIV plan.
medicationSafety: Sedatives and opioids can worsen hypoventilation; use only when clinically indicated and ordered with close monitoring.
redFlags: Worsening respiratory acidosis per ordered testing
teaching: Explain that the team watches breathing effort and carbon dioxide as well as oxygen.
delegationScope: NIV settings and blood-gas interpretation/escalation are qualified-clinician responsibilities; PN/LVN focuses on monitoring and reporting.
examTrap: Assuming an SpO2 improvement proves ventilation is corrected.
oneLinePearl: Oxygenation can improve while ventilation still fails.
sourceBasis: ERS/ATS NIV guideline for acute respiratory failure

title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula: Comfortable Does Not Mean Stable
bottomLine: High-flow nasal cannula can improve oxygen delivery and reduce work of breathing in selected patients, but persistent tachypnea, escalating oxygen requirement, fatigue, altered mental status, or hemodynamic instability can signal treatment failure.
recognize: A patient may look more comfortable while still requiring increasing support or showing worsening physiologic reserve.
priorities: Trend respiratory effort, support requirements, mental status, and hemodynamics rather than judging success from comfort alone.
assessMonitor: Monitor ordered flow/oxygen settings, saturation, respiratory rate/work, skin/nasal tolerance, secretions, and trajectory.
interventions: Maintain humidification/device setup per protocol and escalate increasing support needs.
medicationSafety: Do not use sedatives to suppress distress that may represent support failure.
teaching: Explain that high flow supports breathing but may need escalation if the illness worsens.
delegationScope: HFNC settings and escalation are respiratory/medical competency dependent; PN/LVN role is focused monitoring and authorized supportive care.
examTrap: Assuming HFNC cannot fail because the patient is not wearing a tight mask.
oneLinePearl: Trend the work and support requirement—not just the saturation.
sourceBasis: American Thoracic Society acute respiratory-failure support principles

title: NIV Alarm: Assess the Patient Before the Machine
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A NIV alarm can represent patient deterioration, disconnection, major leak, obstruction, secretion burden, or device malfunction. Look at the patient first, then trace the interface and circuit.
recognize: Alarm plus distress, cyanosis, silence/loss of airflow, displaced mask, kinked tubing, or disconnected circuit requires immediate response.
priorities: Assess breathing and consciousness, ensure support is reaching the patient, and call respiratory support if the cause is not immediately clear.
assessMonitor: Check interface position, tubing connections, visible obstruction/condensation, device messages, and clinical response.
interventions: Correct simple external disconnections within competency and use backup oxygen/ventilation response per emergency protocol if support is lost.
medicationSafety: Do not silence alarms repeatedly to permit sleep or medication administration without resolving their cause.
teaching: Tell the patient to call for help if the mask or tubing comes off rather than trying unfamiliar device changes.
delegationScope: Alarm response begins with all caregivers; device-setting changes require trained personnel.
examTrap: Silencing the alarm before checking the patient.
oneLinePearl: Patient first, circuit second, settings last.

title: NIV Claustrophobia: Coach Before You Sedate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Fear and claustrophobia can make NIV intolerable. Calm coaching, explanation, positioning, interface adjustment, and respiratory-team support are safer first responses than reflexively sedating a patient whose respiratory drive and airway protection already matter.
recognize: Panic, pulling at mask, tachypnea from anxiety, inability to coordinate, or repeated refusal can be interface-intolerance cues.
priorities: Differentiate anxiety from true worsening respiratory failure, stay with the patient, explain the purpose, and enlist respiratory support.
assessMonitor: Monitor breathing effort, oxygenation/ventilation, mental status, panic triggers, and response to coaching/interface adjustment.
interventions: Use short instructions, reassurance, breaks only when clinically safe/ordered, and alternative interface strategies through qualified staff.
medicationSafety: Sedation can worsen hypoventilation, airway protection, and delirium; it requires a specific indication/order and appropriate monitoring.
redFlags: Anxiety accompanied by worsening physiologic distress
teaching: Explain the sensation expected from positive pressure and how to signal for help.
delegationScope: Supportive coaching is within general care; sedative decisions and NIV setting/interface changes are competency dependent.
examTrap: Giving a sedative solely because the patient says the mask feels frightening.
oneLinePearl: First ask whether the patient is frightened—or failing ventilation.

title: Positive-Pressure Comfort: Prevent Dryness and Pressure Injury Without Losing Support
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Dry mouth/nose, eye irritation, skin pressure, and secretion thickening can reduce tolerance of NIV/HFNC. Address humidification, oral/nasal care, interface fit, and skin protection through the prescribed device plan while preserving effective respiratory support.
recognize: Cracked lips, dry mucosa, thick secretions, nasal irritation, eye dryness, facial redness, and device intolerance are common supportive-care needs.
priorities: Assess the cause and device fit rather than simply reducing prescribed support.
assessMonitor: Inspect oral/nasal mucosa, skin contact points, secretion quality, hydration status, and comfort.
interventions: Provide mouth/skin care and prescribed humidification/interface protection; involve respiratory therapy for device-related problems.
medicationSafety: Avoid unapproved topical products that interfere with mask seals or carry fire risk around oxygen-rich environments.
teaching: Report pain, burning, severe dryness, or skin breakdown early.
delegationScope: Basic comfort care may be delegated; device settings and interface changes require trained oversight.
examTrap: Reducing oxygen/pressure independently because the patient has dry mouth.
oneLinePearl: Treat the comfort problem without silently reducing the respiratory treatment.

title: Transport on NIV or HFNC: Plan the Support Before Moving the Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Patients dependent on NIV or HFNC can deteriorate if support is interrupted during transport. Confirm destination readiness, oxygen/power/device capability, monitoring, emergency backup, and responsible personnel before moving the patient.
recognize: High support requirement, recent deterioration, limited oxygen reserve, battery/oxygen limits, or destination equipment mismatch increase transport risk.
priorities: Verify the transport plan and ensure the required level of monitoring and respiratory support accompanies the patient.
assessMonitor: Trend clinical stability immediately before, during, and after transfer.
interventions: Use an approved transport device/oxygen source and emergency backup plan; avoid unnecessary disconnections.
medicationSafety: Coordinate time-sensitive medications without compromising respiratory monitoring or device continuity.
redFlags: Unstable patient without appropriate transport team
teaching: Tell the patient what will happen during transfer to reduce panic and mask removal.
delegationScope: Transport staffing and device management depend on acuity and policy; an unstable NIV/HFNC patient requires appropriately trained personnel.
examTrap: Disconnecting high-flow support for a routine wheelchair transfer because the trip is short.
oneLinePearl: The transport plan must preserve the same life-support need that exists at the bedside.
